strengths: Addresses an important and relatively under-explored problem: tool-augmented, multi-step geospatial reasoning over remote sensing data rather than one-shot perception.

Builds a substantial multimodal corpus (14,538 training / 1,169 evaluation instances; ~100K training reasoning steps) spanning RGB, SAR, GIS layers, and spectral indices such as NDVI/NBR/NDBI across several application domains.
Proposes a unified tool registry and supervised fine-tuning pipeline with response-only masking and deterministic replay of tool calls to verify executability and argument consistency.

Reports both step-by-step and end-to-end evaluations, comparing several frontier and open-source LLMs; OpenEarthAgent-4B shows clear gains in tool selection, argument formatting, and tool-order fidelity over zero-shot baselines on the proposed benchmark.
The supplementary material provides tool I/O schemas, qualitative examples, and the evaluation prompt, which improves transparency relative to a purely high-level description.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core training approach is standard supervised fine-tuning on LLM-generated reasoning trajectories using existing tools and datasets; no new architecture, learning algorithm, or inference-time reasoning mechanism is introduced.

No empirical comparison to prior geospatial agent frameworks such as ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent, or Geo-OLM. The baselines are general-purpose LLMs evaluated zero-shot, so the paper does not establish that OpenEarthAgent is better than existing agentic EO systems.

The benchmark is generated from the same data-construction pipeline and source distribution as the training set; there is no external benchmark, held-out geographic split, or cross-dataset generalization evaluation. Region/source leakage between train and test is not ruled out.

End-to-end performance remains low: non-generative answer accuracy is only ~45%, and the model does not beat GPT-4o on generation accuracy. This weakens claims of robust, verifiable geospatial reasoning in realistic tasks.

Dataset quality and validation are not fully demonstrated: training queries and traces are synthesized by an LLM, and validation is mainly executable replay/argument-format checking rather than logic correctness. Rejection rates, hallucination rates, and inter-annotator agreement are not reported.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no released code, data, trained model, or tool implementations are indicated; training details are incomplete (e.g., gradient accumulation, seeds, number of runs), and no variance or confidence intervals are reported.

Presentation and clarity problems: missing table reference (“Table ??”), duplicated text (“and a batch size of 16. and a batch size of 16”), inconsistent metric names/definitions, and insufficient explanation of how some scores (e.g., Fig. 7 category scores vs Table 4 F1) are computed.
Licensing, privacy, and societal-impact issues for satellite imagery and POI data are not discussed, and limitations of the proposed benchmark and agent are largely omitted.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: tool-augmented multi-step geospatial reasoning over optical, SAR, GIS, and spectral data.
Provides a sizeable curated corpus (14,538 training and 1,169 evaluation instances) with over 100K reasoning steps, covering multiple domains and tool types.
Introduces a unified tool registry and structured reasoning traces that support interpretable, executable multi-step workflows.

Experimental results show that fine-tuning a 4B model improves tool selection, argument validity, and tool-order fidelity over its base model, and is competitive with much larger zero-shot models on several step-by-step metrics.
weaknesses: No explicit contribution type is declared; if judged as Algorithms/General, novelty is limited because the core method is supervised fine-tuning on LLM-generated trajectories plus an existing ReAct/OpenThinkIMG-style tool loop, rather than a new algorithm or learning formulation.

The paper does not directly compare against recent EO agent frameworks such as ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent, or Geo-OLM under the same tools, benchmark, or training protocol; Table 1 is only qualitative, so claims of competitive performance relative to recent agents are not empirically established.

There are no ablations isolating the contributions of the reasoning traces, tool registry, execution cache, response-only masking, or data scale; it is therefore unclear whether gains come from the proposed framework or simply from in-domain supervised fine-tuning.

Baseline fairness is questionable: only OpenEarthAgent is fine-tuned on the tool-use corpus, while open-source baselines are evaluated zero-shot without comparable tool-schema training; no controlled fine-tuned baseline across other backbones is provided.

Several claims appear overstated or inconsistent. End-to-end final answer accuracy is only 45.26, and image-generation success is 75.86, below GPT-4o's 77.93; step-by-step summarization is 83.64, below o4-mini and GPT-4o. The text also cites 45.26 as answer accuracy in the step-by-step section even though that value appears in the end-to-end table.

Dataset quality and validation are not fully convincing. Training trajectories are generated by an LLM and are not manually verified; automated validation mainly checks executability, formatting, and spatial consistency rather than semantic correctness of the reasoning or final answer. Test-set manual inspection is not accompanied by agreement statistics or error rates.

Evaluation robustness is limited. Final answers are partly judged by gpt-4o-mini with a ±10% tolerance and no validation of the judge, and the supplementary evaluation prompt as provided appears malformed, making the scoring protocol hard to reproduce or trust.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code, dataset release, or access details are stated; external tool implementations and models (e.g., TextToBbox, ObjectDetection, ChangeDetection, segmentation, index computation) are unspecified, along with versions, seeds, prompts, and licensing details for GEE/OSM-derived layers.

Methodological details are underspecified. Equation 3 optimizes only the tool-action policy, and it is unclear whether thought tokens are actually supervised. The framework also trains only on validated successful trajectories, so there is no demonstrated learning of error recovery despite the supplementary error analysis.

Benchmark design and metrics have weaknesses: final task success is inconsistently evaluated, with image-generation tasks judged by tool-call success rather than answer correctness; tool-order metrics can be high while final answer accuracy remains low; and the data split is highly imbalanced, with only 223 training and 123 evaluation index-based examples despite broad claims about spectral/index reasoning.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important gap: tool-augmented, interpretable geospatial reasoning over multimodal Earth observation data that combines RGB/SAR imagery, GIS layers, and spectral indices.

Provides a substantial curated corpus: 14,538 training and 1,169 evaluation instances with over 100K reasoning steps, spanning urban, disaster, environmental, infrastructure, and other thematic domains.

Introduces a unified tool registry and orchestration scheme with JSON contracts, tool execution caching, and supervised fine-tuning over validated reasoning trajectories, enabling structured multi-step workflows.

Reports broad empirical comparisons against frontier and open-source LLMs, and the 4B OpenEarthAgent model achieves strong tool-selection, argument-name, argument-value, and tool-order metrics, especially on GIS- and index-based tasks.
Includes qualitative examples and error analysis that illustrate zero-shot multi-step geospatial workflows and highlight common failure modes such as syntax errors and redundant tool calls.
The paper positions itself clearly against prior EO agent frameworks and demonstrates the value of domain-specific supervision for geospatial tool use.
weaknesses: The core contribution is largely a data-construction pipeline plus supervised fine-tuning; there is limited algorithmic or theoretical novelty beyond adapting existing tool-agent principles to geospatial data.

Evaluation is restricted to the self-constructed benchmark. There are no results on existing EO-agent benchmarks or direct comparisons to methods such as ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent, or Geo-OLM, so generalization and external validity remain unproven.

Many tool implementations and dependencies are not specified. Perceptual, OCR, image-description, change-detection, and search tools likely rely on external models or APIs, making reproducibility and the claimed deterministic replay questionable.

The dataset is heavily LLM-synthesized and automatically validated, with manual inspection only on the test set. There is no reported inter-annotator agreement, hallucination analysis, or tool-output quality audit for the training data.

Final answer accuracy is still modest (45.26% Ans.; 83.64% Summ.) and summarization accuracy is below frontier models. Claims of consistent improvements need qualification and the text/table reporting has inconsistencies.

Ablations are limited: there is little analysis of data scale, trajectory filtering, tool-registry effects, loss masking, or training-run variance, and only a small supplement compares two base models.
Answer accuracy is judged by an LLM (gpt-4o-mini) whose reliability is not validated; this introduces potential evaluation bias and reduces confidence in the headline task-level results.
There is no explicit code/data release statement, and no limitations or societal-impact discussion, which weakens reproducibility and responsible-development assessment.
The benchmark split is relatively small (1,169 samples), and per-category coverage is not reported in sufficient detail to judge robustness across all geospatial tasks and regions.

strengths: Presents a large, diverse EO-agent corpus with 14,538 training and 1,169 evaluation instances, 107K reasoning steps, and explicit tool-call traces spanning GIS, spectral, RGB, SAR, and GeoTIFF operations.

The unified tool registry and deterministic replay validation are a useful engineering contribution, standardizing heterogeneous geospatial operators under a consistent JSON schema and enabling cache-based reuse and validation.

Evaluation is broad, covering frontier and open-source LLMs in step-by-step and end-to-end modes, with ablations on data composition, in-context learning, tool-schema exposure, tool ordering, and high-level planning.

The 4B OpenEarthAgent model achieves strong tool-call validity, parameter-name accuracy, GIS/perception F1, and tool-order fidelity, demonstrating that a compact specialized model can outperform much larger general LLMs on structured geospatial tool use.
The paper provides useful supplementary detail on tool I/O, judge prompts, cross-benchmark evaluation, error analysis, and domain-stratified performance, which improves transparency.
If viewed primarily as a dataset/benchmark contribution, the corpus and execution framework fill a real gap between perception-centric EO models and tool-augmented geospatial reasoning.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the core approach is supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3-4B on synthesized tool-use trajectories, building on existing ReAct/tool-agent and OpenThinkIMG-style ideas rather than introducing a new reasoning or learning algorithm.

The paper does not empirically compare against the specialized geospatial agent baselines it positions against, such as ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent, RS-Agent, or Geo-OLM, on its own benchmark; Table 1 is qualitative and the cross-benchmark evaluation lacks the original Earth-Agent method.

The dataset and reasoning traces are largely LLM-generated and automatically validated, with no reported human audit of training trace correctness, inter-annotator agreement, or rejection/regeneration rates; this weakens claims about reasoning fidelity and spatial correctness.

Absolute final-answer performance is low (45.26% answer accuracy), and argument-value accuracy is only 62.10%, meaning a substantial fraction of tool parameters are still wrong; this undercuts claims of reliable spatially grounded execution.

Summarization accuracy is not state-of-the-art: OpenEarthAgent scores 83.64, below o4-mini's 89.48 and only marginally above the Qwen3 baseline's 83.28, limiting the strength of the final-answer reasoning claim.

Comparisons may be unfair: the fine-tuned specialized 4B model is contrasted with generic LLMs not trained on the same trajectories; although an ICL ablation helps, it does not fully establish that baseline prompting was optimized comparably.

The benchmark is self-constructed from the same pipeline used to generate training data, so there is a risk of template leakage and schema-specific bias; evidence of generalization to truly independent geospatial tasks is limited.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: code and models are promised but not released, and the pipeline depends on external services/data such as Google Earth Engine and OpenStreetMap, with no detailed licensing or long-term availability discussion.
There is no substantive limitations or societal-impact discussion, and no statistical significance/variance analysis across multiple random seeds for the main comparisons.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and important problem: tool-augmented multi-step geospatial reasoning over remote sensing data.

It introduces a sizable curated corpus (14,538 training / 1,169 evaluation instances, ~100K reasoning steps) spanning optical, SAR, GIS, and spectral/index tasks; this could be a useful resource if properly released and maintained.

The unified tool registry, JSON-based callable schema, and deterministic replay validation are sensible engineering choices that help standardize heterogeneous GIS/RS tools and support executable trajectories.

The fine-tuned 4B model improves several tool-call validity metrics (e.g., Inst./Tool./ArgN./ArgV.) and GIS/perception F1 over general open baselines, and the paper includes supplementary ablations on data composition, tool schema, tool order, and high-level planning.
The writing is generally clear, with helpful figures and tables illustrating the pipeline and example reasoning traces.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited for ECCV: the method is essentially supervised fine-tuning of an LLM on tool-use trajectories, combining existing agentic paradigms (ReAct/OpenThinkIMG) with existing EO agent ideas (ThinkGeo/Earth-Agent). There is no new learning algorithm, no theoretical analysis, and no major architectural innovation.

The experimental comparison is not adequately controlled. OpenEarthAgent is fine-tuned on in-domain tool trajectories and tool schemas, while most baselines are zero-shot general LLMs (or the same Qwen3-4B base without fine-tuning). The reported gains therefore largely reflect supervised adaptation to the benchmark rather than a methodological advance.

Strong relevant baselines are missing. The paper does not compare against fine-tuned/agentic EO systems such as Earth-Agent, ThinkGeo, or Geo-OLM under matched data, tools, and compute; comparisons to raw GPT-4o/GPT-5/o4-mini do not establish state of the art for tool-augmented geospatial reasoning.

Dataset quality and validation are not convincingly established. Queries and reasoning traces are LLM-generated; automatic validation mainly checks executability/syntax rather than semantic correctness. Only the test set is said to receive manual inspection, and no human evaluation/inter-annotator agreement or training-trace error rate is reported.

Several tools are non-deterministic or externally dependent (e.g., OCR, object detection, change detection, GoogleSearch, Google Earth Engine, OpenStreetMap). This undermines claims of deterministic execution/replay and makes ground-truth answers and evaluation dependent on external services that can change over time.

The evaluation protocol is weak. Answer accuracy is judged by an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini) without human validation, confidence intervals, seeds, or variance reports. The supplementary open-source judge check only shows ranking consistency, not correctness. Metrics across models are not normalized for prompting/tool exposure.

The claims overreach the evidence. For example, GPT-4o remains better on Operation F1 and Generation Accuracy, Logic F1 and Answer Accuracy are still low (51.18 and 45.26), and tool-order fidelity is only around 67-73%. The claimed state-of-the-art and consistent improvements are not fully supported.

There is an unexplained inconsistency between the main accuracy numbers (Ans. 45.26, Gen. 75.86) and the supplementary model-selection table (Ans. 23.47, Gen. 90.76). This raises concerns about clarity, consistency, and reproducibility of the reported results.

Reproducibility and release are not yet sufficient. Code/models are only promised, with no dataset license, datasheet, versioning, or artifact link. The method executes model-generated Python for Solver/Plot/Calculator without describing sandboxing, which is a security/reproducibility risk.

The benchmark may be biased toward the proposed pipeline because training and test examples come from the same LLM-based generation process, prompt templates, and tool distributions. Only one external benchmark (Earth-Agent) is tried, and no contamination analysis is provided.

Key ablations (data composition, in-context learning, tool schema, tool order, high-level planning) are mostly in the supplementary material. The tool-schema ablation in particular suggests that maximal JSON exemplars and schema engineering drive much of the gain, weakening the algorithmic contribution.
Important limitations and societal-impact/dual-use discussions are absent, despite the fact that the data and agent operate on geospatial surveillance, disaster, and infrastructure analysis tasks.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: tool-augmented, multi-step geospatial reasoning over remote sensing data, where current VLMs remain largely descriptive and one-shot.

Introduces a unified executable tool registry covering perceptual, GIS, spectral, georeferenced-raster, and utility tools, with deterministic replay validation to enforce executable and spatially consistent reasoning traces.

Provides a substantial and diverse agentic corpus: 14,538 training instances and 1,169 evaluation instances, with over 107K reasoning steps spanning urban, environmental, disaster, infrastructure, transportation, aviation, and related domains, including RGB, SAR, GIS, and multispectral/index-based tasks.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: step-by-step and end-to-end protocols, comparisons with frontier and open-source LLMs, tool-order metrics, category-wise analyses, and supplementary ablations on data composition, in-context learning, tool schema, tool ordering, and high-level planning.

The core empirical claim is well supported: the 4B OpenEarthAgent model substantially improves over its Qwen3-4B baseline and achieves strong tool-selection, argument, and tool-order performance, often competitive with much larger frontier models.
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed through detailed training setup, tool I/O tables, evaluation prompts, listed data sources, and promised public release of code and trained models.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: the framework is primarily supervised fine-tuning on curated trajectories with a standardized tool interface, rather than a new learning algorithm or architectural innovation; it is closely related to prior agentic EO frameworks such as ThinkGeo and Earth-Agent.

The reasoning traces are largely synthesized by an LLM-based pipeline with automated validation; only the test set is explicitly manually inspected, so training traces may contain annotation artifacts, limited semantic diversity, and unquantified geographic or task biases.

End-to-end final-answer accuracy remains modest (45.26% answer accuracy; 83.64% step-wise summarization), and the model still trails the strongest reasoning baselines on final summarization, indicating that fully robust geospatial reasoning is not yet solved.

Answer accuracy depends on an LLM judge (GPT-4o-mini), and although supplementary checks show rank consistency with an open-source judge, the protocol may still be sensitive to prompt design, calibration, and judge-specific bias.

Direct comparisons to some closely related geo-agent systems on the proposed benchmark are limited, and the paper does not fully ablate whether gains come from the tool schema, the dataset, or the base model's pre-existing capabilities.
The main paper does not substantially discuss limitations, dataset licensing, geographic coverage, societal impact, or potential dual-use risks of geospatial monitoring agents.
